subject: High execution time and Combiner usage

messages.author: 4f28c616429e760d
messages.subject: High execution time and Combiner usage
parts:
Hi,
 
I have been running a sample Rhipe job to calculate betas using OLS. The code runs perfectly fine(validated results using lm() ) with combiner = FALSE. For about ~300mb of data it took about ~17 minutes, which is very high. So, I decided to use combiner(combiner=TRUE) but, I am getting an error. My understanding is that whatever we define in reduce function (as in pre, reduce, post and not reduce expression) will be used as combiner function. 
 
I ran this using Rhipe_0.73.1 on a 11 node cluster(fairly good configuration).
 
(It is also worthwhile to note that I tried to run this same program using another package, with & without using combiner, it took ~3 minutes.)
 
Below is the code and error.
 
Error: Error in solve.default(as.matrix(x), as.matrix(y)) :
         ' b' must be compatible with 'a'
Code:
 
library(Rhipe)
rhinit()
map<- expression({

        datMat<- do.call("rbind", lapply(map.values, function(r){
                as.numeric(strsplit(r, ",")[[1]])
        }))
        yMat<- as.matrix(datMat[,4])
        datMat<- cbind(1, as.matrix(datMat[, c(5,6,7)]))
        val1 <- crossprod(datMat, datMat)
        val2 <- crossprod(datMat, yMat)
        rhcollect("temp_out",cbind(val1,val2))
}
)
reduce<- expression(
        pre = {vals<- 0},
 
        reduce = {vals<- Reduce("+", reduce.values)},
 
        post={
        x <- vals[, -dim(vals)[2]]
        y <- vals[, dim(vals)[2]]
        betas<- solve(as.matrix(x), as.matrix(y))
        rhcollect("betas", betas)})
 
z <- rhwatch(map=map
                ,reduce=reduce,
                ,input=rhfmt(<input>,type='text')
                ,output=rhfmt(<output>,type='text')
                ,jobname = "Rhipe_OLS"
                ,read=FALSE)
rhread(z,type="text")

parts:
This is the code I used. I too had 3 map tasks (388MB). And 1 reduce.
It took 60 seconds.

This computer has 8 cores, and 16GB ram. The job ran on 3 different nodes and data locality was 100%.

Rgds
Saptarshi


## #############################
## Code to generate data
## #############################
map <- expression({
  lapply(map.values,function(i){
    y <- matrix(runif(7*1000),ncol=7)
    apply(y,1,function(r) rhcollect(NULL,r))
  })
})
datMat <- rhwatch(map=map,reduce=1, input=c(3000,10)
                  ,output=rhfmt(type='text',folders="/user/sguha/tmp/txt",writeKey=FALSE)
                  ,read=FALSE)

## ######################################
## LM code
## ######################################
map<- expression({
  datMat<- do.call("rbind", lapply(strsplit(unlist(map.values)," "),as.numeric))

yMat<- as.matrix(datMat[,4])
  datMat<- cbind(1, as.matrix(datMat[, c(5,6,7)]))
  val1 <- crossprod(datMat, datMat)
  val2 <- crossprod(datMat, yMat)
  rhcollect("temp_out",cbind(val1,val2))
})

reduce<- expression(
pre = { .sum <- 0},

reduce = { for(x in reduce.values) .sum <- .sum +x},
    post={
      if(.rhipe.current.state == "map.combine"){

rhcollect( reduce.key, .sum)
      }else{
        x <- .sum[, -dim(.sum)[2]]
        y <- .sum[,  dim(.sum)[2]]
        betas <- solve(as.matrix(x), as.matrix(y))
        rhcollect("betas", betas)
      }
    })

z <- rhwatch(map=map ,reduce=reduce,combine=TRUE
             ,input=rhfmt("/user/sguha/tmp/txt",type='text')
             ,jobname = "Rhipe_OLS",mapred=list(mapred.reduce.tasks=1))

messages.author: 5b0c9158bfa781ba
messages.subject: Re: [rhipe] High execution time and Combiner usage
parts:
Hello,

The concept of Reduce(also called Fold) as been present since the dawn of
CS. Google/Hadoop's MapReduce  takes this to a distributed level (and quite a
marvel it is).

The map function sends as output values tagged by keys. No function is applied
to the values. However the keys are 'partitioned'. As an example, consider
integer keys and mapred.reduce.tasks(R) set to 100. Then the partitioner function
is applied to these integer keys

Partitioner(key) = key modulo R

Thus however many distinct integer keys the map produces, each emitted key/value
pair get's assigned to one of the R reducers. That is, all emitted KV pairs with
Partitioner(key) equal to 0 modulo R is assigned to one reducer. If the map
outputs a million records, these records get assigned to 100 different buckets
(not necessarily equally distributed across the R buckets, that depends on the
key distribution).

So far the reducer is an abstract concept. All the values that share the same
exact key get "Reduced". If a cluster Rc computers, these R buckets are assigned
to the Rc computers.

Now the reduce begins. Let {V1,V2,...,Vn} be the values emitted by the map that
share the same _exact_ key. If you read the Wikipedia page for Reduce/Fold,
let's called the function F, then the output is (for a left reduce)

F(...F(F(F(startValue,V1),V2),V3))

That is take a startValue, apply F to that and the first incoming value, then
take the output and F to that and next value and so on.

So a sum, i.e. 2+3+4+5+...+n is essentially

Sum(Sum(Sum(  Sum(0,2) , 3),4),....) and so on.

Consider the 'min'

Min(Min(Min(Inf,2),3),4)....

and so on.

How does this look in the Java version of the Reduce, see [1],

   public void reduce(Key key, Iterable values,...)
     int sum = 0;
     for (IntWritable val : values) {
       sum += val.get();
     }
     send output to hadoop
   }

That is sum is initialized to 0, then sum is added to the first value, then this
sum is added to the next value.

And that is the Reduce of MapReduce. You might already know this. Note if
operations (e.g. sum/min) are commutative (order doesn't matter) and associative
(arrangement doesn't matter), then you can perform the Reduce on _subsets_ of
the values (sharing the same exact key). Having computed the Reduce on the
subsets we have Foutput1, Foutput2,.... Then the Reduce is applied to Foutput1,
Foutput2, and so on. Consider the sum

2+3+4+5+6+7

is same as (2+3)  + (5+7) + (4+6) (arrangement/order dont matter)
So the reduce is computed on {2,3}, {5,7} and {4,6} (the combiner is doing these
in the map phase). The outputs of these mini reduces are sent to the final
Reduce stage, and the Reduce function reduces {5, 12, 10} to get the final
answer.

If your operations are assoc/commutative, _use_ a combiner!

The R version
-------------

If i had to map R exactly the same way as Java, then rhwatch would take the
following function in reduce parameter

reduce=expression({
        sum  = 0                            ## 1.We got a reduce key
        while(TRUE){
          sum = sum+get.next.reduce.value() ## 2.keep looping to get all values for the key
          if (!has.more.reduce.values?())
            break
        }
                                            ## 3.Done with all reduce values, now write to disk
        rhcollect(reduce.key, sum)
        })

This is *costly* because i have to call a function for _every_ reduce value! In
R, as you might be well aware, if you want performance, you need to vectorize.

So the above now looks like

reduce = expression(
       ## 1. Pre is called _once_ for every reduce key
       pre = { .sum = 0},  

       ## 2. 'reduce' is called  several times, each time reduce.values is a _list_ of the values
       ##    emitted from 'map' (or 'reduce' if a combiner is being used)
       reduce = { .sum = .sum + sum(unlist(reduce.values)) },
      
       ## 3. 'post' is called when _all_ reduce values have been processed (even
       ##    in a combiner). Unless you are _positive_ that "reduce" will only be
       ##    called once, rhcollect should _only_ appear here

       post = { rhcollect(reduce.key, .sum)}
       )

Since a sum is commutative and associative, i can use a combiner here. If one
uses the combiner, then the output from the map (the 'shape') should be the same
as the shape from the reduce expression above. This is because, one subsets of
the map output (again sharing the same key), the above reduce expressions are
called. When the map is complete, this output is shuffled,sorted and sent to the
reduce.

Thus the reduce expressions are called _again_ on the output it returned in
map/combiner stage.

For another example, my input data set has

userID, timestamp, x

I want to keep the first 1000 rows for each userID sorted by time(e.g. the first
1000 calls).

map = expression({
  rhcollect(userID, data.frame( userid=userid, ts=timestamp, x=x))
  })
NUM = 1000
reduce = expression(
   pre = { dfkeep = NULL },
   reduce = {
          ## reduce.values is a list of shape list( userid=userid, ts=timestamp, x=x)
          ## where userid is the same for every element in the list, since
          ## userid is the key
          dfkeep = rbind(dfkeep, do.call(rbind, reduce.values))
          dfkeep = head(df[order(df$ts),],NUM)
          },
   post = { rhcollect(reduce.key, dfkeep) }
   )

(* data frames are conceptually easier, for performance one might use lists,
though the code is more complicated)

The above code can be used with a combiner, since the essential operation is a
'min'. When the reduce gets a new user id, dfkeep is assigned to NULL. The
'reduce$reduce' is called with a list of  list( userid=userid, ts=timestamp,
x=x), which are rbinded into one big data frame. The first NUM obs are kept and
in 'post' written out.  If no combiner were used, then _all_ the values for the
userid would be sent to one reduce computer, the reduce$reduce would be called
repeatedly. This is wasteful. Instead by using a combiner, the above is called
on subsets of the rows (corresponding to the same user id).

If one uses a combiner, it _sometimes_ useful to have different operations
depending on whether the above reduce code is called in the combine stage or the
reduce stage. The main difference is that when the code is called in the reduce
stage, the rhcollect sends data to the final output folder. When the above code
is called in the Combine stage, the output is sent to the Reducer.

In the reduce expression, to know if the code is being called in the Combine
mode .rhipe.current.state is set to 'map.combine'. When the reduce code is being
called in the final Reduce stage(of the MapReduce dance), then
.rhipe.current.state is set to 'reduce'. I dont encourage using these variables
- it makes code confusing.

Lastly, the biggest hit in the reduce (in it's current implementation) is when
you have billions of unique keys, each with a handful of values. The the
reduce$pre, reduce$reduce,reduce$post invocation sequence becomes costlier than
the actual useful execution time. I haven't come up with a good way to get
around this (assuming the user doesn't make any guarantees)


I hope this helps. Feel free to ask questions. if you can produce reproducible
code, that helps too.

Regards
Saptarshi
